newsitem.title: USA: US derivatives industry praises Greenspan remarks.
newsitem.headline: US derivatives industry praises Greenspan remarks.

text.p: U.S. derivatives industry participants praised U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's comments that government regulations of derivatives markets should be re-examined to make sure of their usefulness.
"In today's complex world of financial transactions, one size of regulation does not fit all," Chicago Mercantile Exchange chairman Jack Sandner said in a statement.

"Under the CFTC's model," he said, "every kind of constituency from the most professional institutional trader to the widow in South Dakota must fall under the same regulatory scheme, which is built for the widow and not for the pension funds, mutual funds and institutions."
The Chicago Board of Trade said Greenspan's comments regarding the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) supported calls for less regulation for U.S. futures exchanges.
"He is right in saying that we already have enough regulation," CBOT chairman Patrick Arbor said in the exchange's statement.
Greenspan, speaking in Florida at a conference sponsored by the Atlanta Fed on Friday, said Congressional efforts to reform parts of the CEA have raised contentious issues.
In some cases, there is no need to apply government regulation because the parties involved already were managing risks effectively, Greenspan said.

One swaps dealer said of Greenspan's remarks, "He is saying in effect we don't need the government to step in and do anything because the market incentives are so strong for these people to do them well themselves."

U.S. futures exchanges, including the CBOT, have testified for Congressional legislation calling for less oversight by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates exchange-traded futures under the CEA.
They contend that CFTC regulations are burdensome and expensive, and could result in a decline in exchange business as investors shift to the over-the-counter markets.
A bill crafted by Senators Richard Lugar and Patrick Leahy would require the CFTC to analyze the costs and benefits of any new regulation.

Mark Brickell, managing director of J.P. Morgan and a board member of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association, said Greenspan's comments were likely to add momentum to the Lugar-Leahy bill.
John Frawley, chairman of the Managed Futures Association, also said Greenspan's comments might affect lawmakers' decisions when they vote on the bill.
"I have to believe that his comments influence that person who's on the fence," Frawley told reporters in Washington.
Greenspan also said the CEA may not be the best way to regulate off-exchange transactions with retail investors.

"Some government regulation of off-exchange transactions with such counterparties may be appropriate," Greenspan said. "But, even for those transactions, it is not obvious that the CEA provides the best regulatory framework." ((Derivatives desk 312-408-8750;E-mail derivatives@reuters.com))
